posts.title: Tiny dog. Wild ancestry.
posts.caption:
Tiny dog, unexpected family history. 🐕

A genetic study found traces of coyote ancestry in Chihuahuas, estimated at roughly 0.1% of their genome. The link appears to come from interbreeding between coyotes and ancestors of domestic dogs long ago.

That does not mean a Chihuahua is a miniature coyote. Researchers say this small genetic contribution probably does not explain the breed’s bold personality. More research is needed to pin down the ancestral connection.

Source: Smithsonian · 18 Nov 2026
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/chihuahuas-seem-to-carry-a-tiny-bit-of-coyote-dna-but-thats-probably-not-why-they-have-fearless-personalities-180989886/

posts.title: Earth’s missing chapters
posts.caption:
Earth’s history has missing chapters. 🪨

In some places, gaps in the rock record span more than a billion years. This geological puzzle is called the Great Unconformity.

New computer simulations suggest a possible sequence: movement deep in the mantle raised ancient continental regions, then ice sheets eroded exposed rock before the land sank again. The study supports a proposed explanation; it does not make every detail of this long-running mystery settled.

The illustration combines geological ideas and is not a reconstruction of a specific ancient landscape.

Source: Smithsonian · 16 Nov 2026
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/more-than-a-billion-years-worth-of-rock-layers-are-missing-from-earths-geologic-record-scientists-say-they-may-finally-know-why-180989870/

posts.title: One life. Two ways to live.
posts.caption:
The shift to farming may have unfolded within one man’s lifetime. 🌾

A new analysis of the approximately 6,000-year-old Rødhals Man, found on a Danish island, suggests his diet changed as he grew up. He ate mostly seafood in childhood, then added more land-based protein from around age 11.

Researchers interpret the evidence as a possible sign that he interacted with early farming communities while retaining parts of a foraging way of life. The scene shown is an imaginative illustration, not a reconstruction of his appearance or home.

Source: Smithsonian · 18 Nov 2026
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/from-a-small-island-in-denmark-this-man-lived-through-the-transition-from-hunter-gathering-to-farming-6000-years-ago-180989889/

posts.title: A tomb with distant connections
posts.caption:
A glass cup believed to be Roman was among 413 artifacts found in a roughly 2,000-year-old Xiongnu tomb in Mongolia. The jade objects, silver pendant and other finds add evidence of far-reaching exchange networks, but they do not reveal the cup's exact journey or prove direct contact between Rome and Mongolia.

Source: Smithsonian Smart News · 20 Nov 2026

posts.title: A second chance for a rare snake
posts.caption:
A bright snake gets a head start. Conservationists released 62 young San Francisco garter snakes after raising them for about a year, giving the endangered animals a better chance of surviving their vulnerable early months. The release supports a wider recovery effort; it does not mean the species has recovered. Exact locations are withheld to protect the snakes.

Source: Smithsonian Smart News · 23 Nov 2026

posts.title: A tiny flower hidden for 100 million years
posts.caption:
Micro-CT X-rays revealed a tiny flower hidden inside a sandstone museum specimen collected in Kansas more than 130 years ago. The roughly 100-million-year-old flower survives as a negative cavity left after the original material decayed. Its structure may point to an extinct palm relative, but that classification remains uncertain.

Source: Phys.org / Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · 23 Nov 2026
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-hidden-million-years-rays-reveal.html

posts.title: The golden burbot
posts.caption:
Most burbot blend into the lake bottom with mottled brown and olive coloring. During a survey of New York’s Oswego Harbor, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service biologists caught one in vivid yellow-orange. The unusual coloring comes from xanthochromism, a rare condition that lets yellow pigment dominate. Burbot are native to the Great Lakes, and this was the first recorded burbot in a fisheries survey of that harbor.

Source: Smithsonian Smart News · 24 Nov 2026
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/biologists-discovere-a-one-in-a-million-bright-yellow-burbot-fish-in-new-yorks-oswego-harbor-180989928/

posts.title: A shadow in the sand
posts.caption:
In 2025, excavators at Sutton Hoo’s Garden Field cemetery uncovered a body-shaped impression preserved in the sand. The acidic soil can dissolve bones and other remains while leaving a trace of their shape. The team also found grave goods and clues that a second person may have been buried there. The timing and relationship of the possible burials remain uncertain.

Source: Smithsonian Smart News · 24 Nov 2026
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/almost-90-years-after-discovering-a-ship-burial-that-rewrote-british-history-archaeologists-returned-to-sutton-hoo-this-time-they-uncovered-a-ghostly-sand-body-180989932/
